Otherwise, it's such a good idea. If we had a way to make sure users couldn't vote multiple times it would be perfect!
How about making requirements for accounts which reach a certain amount of comment contribution points like 25/50/100 in order to vote for mods?
It would still be too easy for them. Plus the more contribution points a vote requires the more you're disadvantaging the lurkers.

One problem there is that the moderator position becomes a popularity contest, which is just a race to the bottom. What is most popular is what's on the front page of reddit. So if you have /v/seriousdiscussion and the users want more cat memes, the mod candidates that promise cat memes take over. Moderators need a fair amount of dictatorial power over their subs in order to maintain them - they can't be at the mercy of the user base.
That is true. Maybe they're could be a head mod (probably the creator of the subverse) that would make rules for what mods could promise.

There's nothing to say that a sub creator couldn't hold a poll for who was a mod. I've seen subs on reddit do this, with calls for nominations from the community. I think the real question is how to force transparency in moderator actions. You can't usurp a mod's powers but maybe you can expose them, somehow.
Maybe the admins could. If the users notice the mods acting unethically, the users could have the admins investigate.

That's an idea but it doesn't scale well. Let's suppose you have a sub with highly technical content. The mod deletes a post as being off topic/against the rules. Now the admin has to sit down and figure out who's right and who's wrong? How does he know? Easiest thing to do is to side with the moderator.
Good point. Maybe their could be a system of checks and balances where mods are ranked.

One problem with that is that people that are happy might not vote but people with a grudge definitely would. The rankings would skew negative, so you'd want to show people who hadn't voted at all as well as those that voted up or down.

Full Disclosure: I paid a hair under market price for this from the Zen Factory Outlet guys at a trade show in Atlanta. Which let me get beer that night.

Maybe I should do Final Thoughts first, just to get the important part out of the way:

Up until the other day, I used this every single day and I love the shit out of this mod. Mostly because it was a unicorn of mine since it came out in January last year. It was the first mod that I ever absolutely needed. It grew on me like a tumor until there, at Vape-a-palooza, it stared me in the face. And I bought it. A splurge for many, a necessary purchase for me to go on living my life as a semifunctional non-Gollum.

I've had DNA 30 devices before this one. I had the Vapor Shark DNA 30, which I sold to help me get enough cash together to get this. Neither has great battery life but at least with the ZNA Lite, I was able to purchase enough (7) AW IMR 18490s to get me through the day of constant vaping.

The Body

The Z2 thread spec is chunky. It's designed for durability in the face of constant use. After having it for nearly 6 months, the threading has definitely held up. It's got a chunk missing in one part, but that doesn't keep it from threading like a dream.

It's got heft. Despite being a bit of a shorty, the stainless steel Zen (Mike) uses is really great, and the anodized aluminum body for the control unit is fantastic as well.

The Top Cap. Notice how I bolded it? That means this upcoming part is super important because it led to me jankifying my positive contact. On recent models, the positive contact is adjustable but it is COUNTER THREADED. It's super soft high quality copper, and I gouged the bejeezus out of it trying to make it screw and unscrew like a normal pin. Counter threaded. That means counter clockwise makes it tighten up, and turning it clockwise makes it loosen. That's very important.

The power adjustment buttons protrude enough, but are a little small. They don't hurt the finger to depress, but aren't necessarily comfy, too. The firing button, though, is super comfy. Using either my thumb or index finger, I haven't had any issues reaching or using it or getting crampy.

Penultimate Impressions

I know exactly what to expect from a DNA chip at this point. Consistency. Absolute consistenty. Every time I hit the button, I know what's about to happen. For the most part, the chip makes a DNA mod, but the ZNA is a little different. The quality makes it first, hence their success with mechanicals, then the chip. Zen could have used any chip in this - Provape's, an SX, whatever, but the DNA chip in this really helps add to it.

I think what I'm getting to is that -- for me -- the ZNA is more than the sum of its parts. It is a gestalt entity, despite its modularity. I love it the way people love their first mods, and the only thing I'll really permanently put this down for is a ZNA 40 Lite.

The Warranty

Keep your receipts, folks. I didn't always feel this way about the ZNA, and one day mine died. Turns out it was a tad janky out of the box resulting in its first death. To submit a warranty return with Zen, you need to have your receipt, but since I got mine at a trade show, I really didn't get one (partly my fault for not opting for one with the Square reader, always do that. Especially if you get arrested.

After I sent in my ZNA for a warranty repair (6 months non transferable for most people), it got to their shop in Spencerport on Friday and was back on my door on Tuesday. Even after it expires, I won't hesitate to send it in for repair.
